note: Typing ( at the end of a line inserts the matching ) and leaves the caret between them.
[ closes itself with ] when followed by end of line.
Typing { at the end of a line inserts } right after the caret.
A ; after the caret still allows the pair, so ( gets its ).
No ) is inserted when the next character is an identifier, so the student can wrap an existing expression by typing the closer later.
A double quote in code inserts its closing quote.
A single quote opens a char literal and closes itself as well.
Typing the closing quote of an auto-closed string steps over the existing quote instead of adding a second one.
The closing ' of a char literal is overtyped.
Typing ) right before an existing ) moves over it.
Only one ) is consumed when two closers follow the caret.
] steps over a following ].
When the next character is not ), typing ) inserts one.
] is inserted normally when the next character is ;.
Inside a string literal a single quote is plain text and gets no partner.
Brackets typed inside a string literal are not paired.
Quotes typed in a // comment are not paired.
After a backslash the quote is an escape: it is inserted and the closing quote stays where it was.
An escaped single quote inside a char literal is inserted, not overtyped.
With a selection, ( wraps it in parentheses and the original text stays selected.
With a selection, " wraps it in quotes and keeps it selected.
At the very start of an empty file the quote still pairs.
Pairing works on the last line of the file with no trailing newline.
Backspace between an empty () removes both.
Backspace between an empty [] removes both.
Backspace between an empty "" removes both quotes.
Backspace between an empty '' removes both quotes.
When the parentheses are not empty only the ( is deleted.
An ordinary character is deleted and the quotes stay.
Only the innermost empty pair is removed.
Backspace at offset 0 changes nothing.
Typing " then Backspace leaves the line as it was.
Enter between {} puts the } on its own line and the caret on an indented blank line between.
Inside main the new body is indented two levels and the } lines up with the for.
A third-level block indents to 12 spaces.
The ; after a struct's } stays attached to the }.
Enter after an opening brace whose } is already on the next line indents one level.
A new line after a statement keeps the block's indent.
After an if header with no brace the next line is indented for its single statement.
A brace-less for header indents the next line one level.
After a block's } the caret returns to the enclosing block's indent.
Enter after the final } at top level gives an unindented line.
Enter in an empty file adds one empty line.
Enter at column 0 pushes the line down and keeps the caret before its text.
Spaces after the caret are dropped; the new line gets the block indent, not the stray spaces.
A preprocessor line at top level gives an unindented new line.
Top-level statements keep column 0.
A helper function above main splits the same way.
Typing { then Enter at the end of a header produces the full three-line block.
A } typed on an indented blank line snaps back to the indent of the block it closes.
Closing main at the end of the file moves the } to column 0.
A } typed at column 0 is indented forward to its block's level as well.
The } lines up with the innermost unclosed for.
Closing a struct body snaps the } to column 0.
The // goes in column 0 and the caret moves to the next line (here clamped to the end of the short } line).
Mod+/ on a commented line removes the // and moves the caret down.
A // after the indent is removed and the indent is kept.
On the last line there is nowhere to move, so the caret stays at the end of the line.
A line that only ends in a comment is still uncommented code, so it gets commented.
Every line the selection touches is commented and the selection stays on the same text.
When every selected line is commented, Mod+/ uncomments them all.
If any selected line is uncommented, all lines get a // prefix, including the one that already had one.
A selection ending at column 0 does not include that line.
A selection within one line comments the whole line and keeps the selection; the caret does not move down.
Nested lines are still commented at column 0, with their indent kept after the //.
Without a selection Mod+D copies the line below and the caret moves to the copy at the same column.
The first line of the file duplicates like any other.
On a last line with no trailing newline the copy goes on a new line.
An empty line duplicates into two empty lines.
With a selection only the selected text is copied, right after itself, and the copy becomes the selection.
A selection of whole lines is copied below itself and the copy is selected.
The copy keeps the original line's indentation.
Alt+Shift+Up swaps the line with the one above and the caret travels with it.
Alt+Shift+Down swaps the line with the one below.
The first line cannot move up, so nothing changes.
The last line cannot move down, so nothing changes.
The last line moves up correctly even without a trailing newline.
Moving down onto a last line without a trailing newline swaps the two lines cleanly.
A selection spanning lines moves all of those lines together and stays selected.
Repeated presses keep moving the same line.
Down then up returns the text and caret to where they started.
Accepting a variable after std:: replaces the typed prefix and adds nothing else.
Typing after std:: narrows the list; accepting cin inserts the name only.
A type name is inserted without parentheses.
A function that takes arguments is inserted with () and the caret between them.
swap takes arguments, so the caret lands inside the parentheses.
getline is inserted as a call with the caret inside.
A member function with a parameter gets () with the caret inside.
A member function with no parameters gets () with the caret after them.
empty() takes nothing, so the caret ends after its parentheses.
back() is a no-argument member call.
Typing after the dot narrows the member list.
String members complete with the same rules.
substr has parameters, so the caret goes between the parentheses.
map::count takes a key, so the caret goes inside.
queue::front completes as a no-argument call.
priority_queue::top completes as a no-argument call.
Inside a string literal no completion popup appears; the text is typed as is.
Inside a // comment no member completion is offered.
